channel.title: Most Fascinating Stories
channel.description: History isn’t defined only by great treaties and epic battles—it turns on the bizarre, the terrifying, and the almost-forgotten coincidences that textbooks left behind. In every episode of Most Fascinating Stories, host Rebecca sets the stage before handing the microphone to a new master storyteller to uncover a true, thoroughly sourced, and dramatized historical event you were never taught in school. Concise 10-to-20 minute deep dives into the unbelievable truths behind humanity’s most famous names and darkest moments.

item.title: Episode 3: Nixon's Midnight Vigil at the Lincoln Memorial
item.description: In May 1970, five days after the Kent State shootings and with Washington D.C. besieged by 100,000 anti-war demonstrators, President Richard Nixon slipped out of the White House unannounced at 4:15 A.M. to speak face-to-face with student protesters at the Lincoln Memorial.

item.title: Episode 2: Eisenhower and the Hellish 1919 Mud Convoy
item.description: In the summer of 1919, Lieutenant Colonel Dwight D. Eisenhower volunteered for the U.S. Army's first transcontinental motor convoy. Across 3,251 miles of dirt, collapsed bridges, and desert quicksand, the grueling two-month ordeal inspired the modern Interstate Highway System.

item.title: Episode 1: FDR and the Friendly Torpedo That Almost Killed Him
item.description: In November 1943, President Franklin D. Roosevelt embarked on a top-secret transatlantic voyage aboard the battleship USS Iowa to meet Churchill and Stalin in Tehran. During live combat exercises, an escort destroyer accidentally launched an armed torpedo directly at the President's ship. Hosted by Rebecca, with story narration by George. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ CHAPTERS: • 00:00 - Intro • 00:47 - Act I: The Cursed Escort • 02:36 - Act II: Depth Charges in the Storm • 04:01 - Act III: Balloons and Blue Skies • 05:16 - Act IV: Fire Two: The Runaway Torpedo • 06:33 - Act V: Wheel Me to the Railing • 08:42 - Act VI: Under Arrest in Bermuda and the Pardon • 10:38 - Conclusion ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ FULL TRANSCRIPT: [Rebecca - Host] Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories, where we uncover the real, documented, and lesser-known tales behind history's most prominent figures. I'm your host, Rebecca. Today, we step into the stormy autumn of nineteen forty-three with President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. We remember FDR for his fireside chats, the New Deal, and steering the Allied powers through World War Two. But history often turns on absurd, razor-thin margins. In November of nineteen forty-three, on a voyage shrouded in total wartime secrecy, an American warship accidentally fired a live, fully armed torpedo directly at the battleship carrying the Commander-in-Chief. And now, here is George with the story. [George - Storyteller] ACT I: THE CURSED ESCORT In the second week of November nineteen forty-three, a thick, cold fog blanketed the waters off Hampton Roads, Virginia. Sliding quietly out into the Atlantic under the cloak of night was the mightiest warship in the United States Navy: the newly commissioned battleship USS Iowa. She was an eighty-eight-thousand-horsepower fortress of steel, carrying nine sixteen-inch guns and armor plates over a foot thick. Aboard was a passenger whose presence was the most closely guarded secret of the war: President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Accompanied by Army Chief of Staff George C. Marshall, Admiral Ernest King, and his closest diplomatic advisers, Roosevelt was embarking on Operation Sextant, crossing the Atlantic to meet Winston Churchill in Cairo and Joseph Stalin in Tehran. It was to be the first face-to-face summit of the Big Three leaders, a meeting that would decide the timing of D-Day and the postwar partition of Europe. For security against German U-boat wolfpacks that infested the Atlantic sea lanes, the Iowa was surrounded by a protective screen of cruisers and destroyers. Among these escorts was a fresh Fletcher-class destroyer: hull number five-seven-nine, the USS William D. Porter, commanded by Lieutenant Commander Wilfred Walter. To her crew of mostly green recruits, the Porter was their ticket to glory. But from the moment she pulled out of Norfolk, the ship seemed cursed with astonishing misfortune. While maneuvering away from the dock, the Porter's stern anchor had hooked onto the railing of a neighboring sister destroyer, ripping away stanchions, railings, and a lifeboat before freeing herself. Captain Walter had delivered a stern dressing-down to his young crew, hoping that humiliating mishap would be their last. It was only the prelude. [George - Storyteller] ACT II: DEPTH CHARGES IN THE STORM Twenty-four hours into the voyage, the convoy ran into ferocious North Atlantic seas. The wind whipped up towering whitecaps, and the destroyers rolled violently in the heavy ocean swells. Suddenly, a massive underwater explosion shook the entire ocean. A thunderous shockwave hammered against the hull of the Iowa. Aboard the battleship, sirens wailed into the storm: General Quarters! Gun crews sprinted to their battle stations; lookout binoculars swept the gray horizons; the Iowa's massive turbines surged to life, heeling the ship into violent zigzag maneuvers. German U-boats were presumed to be attacking the President's flagship. Depth-charge crews stood ready on all destroyers, scanning the foaming waves for periscopes. But there were no German submarines in sight. Minutes later, a shamefaced signal flashed across the water from the William D. Porter. An improperly secured depth charge had rolled off her stern rack during a heavy wave roll and detonated upon reaching its pressure depth. Admiral Ernest King was apoplectic. To broadcast an accidental depth-charge explosion in the middle of the Atlantic was like lighting a flare for every Nazi submarine within a hundred miles. Captain Walter was reprimanded via blinker light, and the men of the Porter hung their heads in disgrace. They desperately needed an opportunity to prove their competence. [George - Storyteller] ACT III: BALLOONS AND BLUE SKIES The opportunity seemed to arrive on Sunday, November fourteenth. The convoy was cruising east of Bermuda, and the weather had cleared into brilliant sunshine and calm blue seas. President Roosevelt, wearing his trademark fedora and clutching a long cigarette holder between his teeth, was brought onto the Iowa's teakwood deck in his wheelchair. He loved the sea; as a former Assistant Secretary of the Navy, Roosevelt was in his element. To entertain the Commander-in-Chief, the Iowa's captain arranged an anti-aircraft gunnery demonstration. Crewmen released large silver weather balloons high into the cloudless sky. Moments later, the Iowa's five-inch, forty-millimeter, and twenty-millimeter guns opened up in a roaring symphony of fire, shredding the silver balloons into ribbons. FDR smiled broadly, puffing his cigarette and applauding the gunnery. Across six thousand yards of open water, Captain Walter of the William D. Porter watched the demonstration. Here was his chance to redeem his ship in the eyes of the President and the high command. Walter ordered his crew to conduct a simulated torpedo drill, using the distant, colossal silhouette of the Iowa as their mock target. [George - Storyteller] ACT IV: FIRE TWO: THE RUNAWAY TORPEDO On the Porter's deck, the torpedo mount was manned by Torpedoman Third Class Lawton Dawson. In a live-fire combat situation, the Mark fifteen torpedoes carried eighteen hundred pounds of high explosives. For a dry drill, Navy regulations strictly mandated that the small explosive primer charges used to expel the torpedoes from their tubes must be removed. Dawson removed the primers from tubes one and three. But on tube number two, in the excitement and noise of the exercise, he made a catastrophic oversight: he left the primer in place. On the bridge, Captain Walter shouted the standard drill command: Mount two, stand by! Fire two! Instead of a hollow metallic click, a terrifying whoosh echoed across the deck. An exhaust plume of white compressed gas billowed into the air. Before the horrified eyes of the crew, a two-ton, fully armed, live torpedo splashed into the Atlantic, its propeller screaming to life at forty-five knots, churning a deadly white frothy wake heading straight for the Iowa. Utter chaos engulfed the bridge of the William D. Porter. Captain Walter stared in disbelief, turning pale as chalk. A live torpedo was speeding directly toward the President of the United States. [George - Storyteller] ACT V: WHEEL ME TO THE RAILING They had less than two minutes before impact. Strict radio silence was in effect to conceal the mission from Axis listening stations. Desperate to warn the Iowa without breaking radio protocols, Walter ordered his signalman to flash an urgent warning with the Aldis lamp. The signalman, shaking with adrenaline, aimed the lamp at the Iowa's towering bridge and began frantically clacking the shutter. Torpedo in water, steer right! he intended to say. Instead, in his blinding panic, the signalman transposed letters. What the Iowa's lookouts read was: Porter is backing up full speed! Aboard the Iowa, the bridge crew blinked in irritation. They flashed back: Porter, clarify message. Seeing that visual signals were failing, Captain Walter threw naval regulations out the window. He grabbed the TBS radio microphone, broke radio silence, and screamed over the fleet's open frequency: Lion, lion, come right! Hard right! Lion, look right! Torpedo in the water! Inside his stateroom, President Roosevelt felt the violent lurch of the deck. Secret Service agent Mike Reilly rushed into the room, shouting that a torpedo was inbound. Most leaders would have ducked for cover inside the conning tower. But Roosevelt's eyes lit up with intense curiosity. Wheel me to the railing, Mike, Roosevelt insisted. I want to see it! Reilly wheeled the President out onto the deck to the starboard railing. With his fedora firmly on his head, Franklin Roosevelt watched the foaming silver track of the torpedo race across the Atlantic directly toward his ship. At the very last moment, the Iowa's sharp evasive turn paid off. The torpedo sliced through the water, missing the stern by roughly twelve hundred yards, detonating in the churning wake. A magnificent geyser of white foam and saltwater erupted hundreds of feet into the sky. The concussion shook the deck of the Iowa, spraying fine ocean mist onto Roosevelt's face. The President let out a low chuckle, removed his cigarette holder, and turned to his aides with a grin. [George - Storyteller] ACT VI: UNDER ARREST IN BERMUDA AND THE PARDON Aboard the Iowa's bridge, however, nobody was smiling. Admiral King and Captain McCrea were utterly convinced they had just survived an assassination plot. Suspicion immediately fell upon the William D. Porter. The Iowa swiveled all nine of her massive sixteen-inch turrets—guns capable of firing twenty-seven-hundred-pound armor-piercing shells twenty miles—and locked them squarely onto the diminutive destroyer. The Porter was ordered to stand down, surrender its logs, and report directly to naval authorities in Bermuda under armed escort. Upon arriving in Bermuda, Marines boarded the William D. Porter and placed the entire crew—officers, sailors, and cooks alike—under military arrest. It was the only time in United States naval history that an entire ship's company was arrested en masse. Interrogations were fierce. Naval intelligence combed through every crewman's background, searching for German saboteurs. Finally, Lawton Dawson, weeping in remorse, confessed that he had inadvertently left the primer in tube number two, and in his panic, had thrown the spent primer casing overboard to hide his mistake. Dawson was court-martialed and sentenced to fourteen years of hard labor. But when the verdict reached the Oval Office, President Roosevelt intervened personally. Writing to the Secretary of the Navy, FDR stated that no harm had been done, that it was clearly an accident born of training frenzy, and asked that Dawson be pardoned and restored to duty. The Navy complied, but they never quite forgave the Porter. The destroyer was exiled to the frozen, fog-choked outpost of the Aleutian Islands. For the remainder of the war, whenever the William D. Porter pulled into a naval anchorage, other American ships would hail her over the radio with the same sardonic joke: Don't shoot, boys, we're Republicans! [Rebecca - Host] CONCLUSION The saga of the William D. Porter remains one of the most astonishing near-misses in modern history. Had that torpedo struck the Iowa's magazine, the course of World War Two—the timing of the cross-channel invasion, the atomic bomb program, and the entire architecture of the postwar world—would have been radically altered in a single blinding flash. Roosevelt's unflappable calm at the railing, asking to be wheeled closer to watch the weapon approach, captures the indomitable spirit of a leader who refused to let fear dictate his life. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time as we unearth another forgotten chapter from the pages of history. Until then, stay curious.
